entries.title: The best books on Battles, recommended by Iain MacGregor
entries.summary: The weapons and tactics of war may change, but the human experience of battle does not, argues Iain MacGregor, author of Battle: The Moments that Transformed Warfare from Ancient Greece to Ukraine. He highlights five books that bring that experience to life, from the ordinary soldier at Agincourt to the brutal realities of the Pacific War and the Falklands. This interview appeared first on Five Bo
entries.content:
In your book, you cover a lot of battles in a lot of places over an extremely long period of time. What did you ultimately conclude?

This is my fifth, and as with all the books I’ve written, it’s not exactly the one I started out writing. Generally, I do people- and story-led books, which relates to two or three of my choices that we’re going to talk about.

This was a diversion. Most historians who are in the genre want to do a book like this because it’s almost like exercising your chops. How much do I know? What are the theories behind it? So I always wanted to do it. You don’t get narrowed down to just one war or battle and 3,000 years of history—that’s exciting.

What I discovered was,  the more research I did—whether it was ancient history, medieval, Tudor, Napoleonic, World War Two—that while the tactics and technology have changed radically, the human dimension is always the same. It’s about human beings.

Whether it’s the commanders, or the line officers on the ground, or the soldiers, they’ve all got the same frailties you and I have got. It doesn’t matter whether they’re a Greek hoplite, a Tudor English sailor, or a Ukrainian soldier on the front line today, you’re still scared. It’s about how you react under pressure. If you’re a commander, it’s about the timing, about how you deal with sudden events.

That hasn’t changed ever, and writing this book over this whole timeline really confirmed that to me.

How much research did you do to cover that many periods?

I’ve edited history books for more than three decades, and military history has been a constant thread throughout my career. Some subjects stay with you. Even when I’m not working on a particular project, I’m always collecting material, whether in notebooks, voice memos, or on my laptop. Over the years I’ve built up tens of thousands of notes on battles, commanders and campaigns. So, when I was asked what I wanted to write, I already had a vast reservoir of research to draw on.

That wasn’t the end of it. For this book I read well over a hundred additional works and revisited many of the battlefields themselves. I’ve walked Civil War sites in Virginia, explored battlefields across Britain, and spent time on key locations in Europe, Russia, Vietnam and Japan. There’s no substitute for standing on the ground, seeing the distances, the terrain and the decisions that commanders had to make.

People often ask how I find the time. The truth is that publishing is already all-consuming; I edit twenty or more books a year. But after enough years, you learn to trust the process. Research accumulates steadily, often unnoticed, until one day you realise you’ve spent decades preparing to write the book that was in your head all along.

OK, so you’ve mentioned reading over 100 books, including all the ones you’ve read over the years. How did you choose these particular five? What were your criteria?

Some were whether they affected how I thought history should be told. I’d say front of that cab rank is John Keegan’s The Face of Battle. It’s probably had more of an influence on me than anything else. A couple of these books are seminal, and I would argue that your readers should definitely go out and read them. Others, like, for instance, With the Old Breed, which we’ll talk about by E.B. Sledge, has got the human factor that I just find gripping. It’s just such a brilliant, raw, emotive, visceral book. It’s not even a memoir—it’s almost like he’s taken it as therapy. It really moved me. Then there are other books that shine a light on aspects of big battles people know about, but hadn’t really thought of them in that way.

Let’s go through each of them and tell me about them, bearing in mind that not everyone may have read them. Let’s start with The Face of Battle (1976) by John Keegan, which covers three battles. Tell me a bit more about the book and and and why it’s so seminal.

John Keegan’s The Face of Battle is arguably the most influential work of military history written in the last fifty years. It radically altered the next generation of published historians coming through.

Before Keegan—and I’ve read a lot of books that came out before—it was always about the great people, generally men of military history. You’re looking at warfare or the battle itself from the top down. You learn about the great strategist who might have won or lost the battle, but not what life was like on the front line for the ordinary person doing the fighting. That’s what Keegan brings to it.

He does it by examining three of the most important battles (from a British perspective) you would want to know about: Agincourt in 1415, Waterloo in 1815, and then the Somme in 1916. These are battles that resonate in every household across Great Britain and further afield. Keegan gives you the background and the context, but he captures them from the ordinary person’s perspective.

What I loved about it when I read it in my early twenties was the fact that it was just so accessible. I thought, ‘He’s writing this for me. This is the way I would like to read history.’ I’ve got dozens of books on my shelf that are very important but they’re very dry—whereas he’s bringing it to life. I mean, in the process of writing my new book, I must have gone back to John’s book at least ten times, because it’s just so good. It’s like a breath of fresh air. I read it again just to get inspired.

With a medieval battle like Agincourt, how do you get the on-the-ground view? There must be a lot more information about the leaders.

With the leaders, you’ve got a lot of material from the time. Then, maybe decades afterwards, you can read about the commanders of the period on both sides, and records showing the casualties.

It’s not that the first-hand material is super scant, but if there’s not much around, you then spread the net slightly wider, and you look at other key battles in the period and how the fighting has been recorded. It’s completely accurate and fair to then add that to whatever work you’re doing.

He’s obviously gone to these places. He’s giving you a bird’s-eye view of the terrain and the weather and what the terrain would be like in that weather.

It gives you an insider’s idea and appreciation of what they were facing. How ferocious was the fighting? Did the tactics work? Did they fail? Was the weather that big of a factor? Was the longbow that big a factor? He brings it to the page in the way that someone like Bernard Cornwell would do in fiction. He really brings it alive, and you want to find out what’s happened to this person he’s writing about, or that unit. That’s what I’ve always found captivating.

One of my colleagues interviewed Antony Beevor about World War Two. She asked him which historian inspired him, and he also mentioned John Keegan, The Face of Battle.

I think if you interviewed any current military historian/author right now, they would say the same thing. There’s no argument. It’s a seminal book. It came out decades ago, but it’s still very much in print.

Let’s turn to your next choice, The Killer Angels (1974) by Michael Shaara. This is set during the American Civil War, and it is actually a novel, is that right?

Yes, it is, but I definitely wanted to bring it in because it’s had just as big of an effect on me as John Keegan’s work has. I am a huge American Civil War researcher and author. I’ve been to quite a few of the battlegrounds in the eastern theatre in Virginia, Maryland and Pennsylvania. I’ve even written a book about it, U.S. Civil War: Battle by Battle.

The Killer Angels is perfect in that Michael Shaara takes Gettysburg, the pivotal battle of the American Civil War, if not in modern American military history, and brings it to life. You can tell he’s done the research because of the way he talks about the units on the move and the planning. The fighting itself at Gettysburg is very, very accurate. The man’s done his homework, but he’s just got that fictional writer’s skill. He just brings to life the drama of the human experience.

You can understand why countless Hollywood producers and directors have read The Killer Angels. At the same time, they’re reading nonfiction books that enable them to picture whatever scene they want to: whether it’s the first, second, or final day of fighting at Gettysburg in July 1863, such as ‘Pickett’s Charge’.

That’s why I think the book is important. You need someone like Michael Shaara because he takes what you might think of as, ‘oh, it’s just military history ’ and he opens it up to a much wider audience. He pulls in a general readership to then study what you could argue are serious nonfiction works about Gettysburg and the wider American Civil War. So, it works on lots of levels.

I was just reading the beginning about the scout checking out where the troops are. It’s very gripping, isn’t it?

Yes. Also, as an editor, what I liked about the book is that he avoids caricatures. He’s writing about the people, the main participants, but he’s not throwing a big bucket of clichés on them. That makes it more believable.

Let’s go to the next book about a battle, which takes us to World War I and Verdun. This is a big favourite in our family. What can you tell me about The Price of Glory (1962) by Alistair Horne?

I’m a recent convert. I was a history lecturer and guide on a cruise around Japan and South Korea in June. I was giving quite a few lectures on Japanese history, which made me realise I wanted to read something that completely took me away from that area, so I could relax. I bought The Price of Glory—I told you I was a military history geek! I thought l’d be having too much of a good time to read the book properly, but I did. I read it cover to cover in six nights.

Can you say a bit about the Battle of Verdun for those who may not be as familiar with it?

The Battle of Verdun was a ten-month-long ordeal in which France and Germany sacrificed hundreds of thousands of men for a few miles of devastated ground. It’s why the Battle of the Somme was necessary to the north, as we, the British, were trying to relieve the pressure on Verdun, which lay to the southeast of our own trenchlines.

Verdun was more than a battlefield. For France, it was a symbol of national survival: a ring of great forts strung across the landscape, long regarded as impregnable. Far from the fighting in Belgium, the sector had been relatively quiet, which was precisely why the Germans chose it. Their aim was not simply to seize ground, but to destroy France’s will to continue the war. As one German commander put it, they would ‘bleed France white’.

The battle opened on 21 February 1916 with one of the heaviest bombardments the world had yet seen. Around a million shells crashed onto French positions on the first day alone. For weeks the Germans seemed unstoppable. Fort after fort came under attack, French units were hurled into the line and shattered by artillery fire, and Verdun became an industrialised slaughterhouse on a scale scarcely imaginable. By the spring of 1916, it appeared possible that the Germans might break through altogether.

Yet Verdun produced the opposite result from the one Berlin expected. Instead of crushing French morale, it hardened it. The battle became a rallying cry for a nation under siege, a test of endurance that France refused to fail. Like the Somme in British memory, Verdun is remembered for its terrible losses, but in France it also carries the meaning of sacrifice, resilience and national defiance. It remains, perhaps more than any other battlefield, part of the military soul of the nation.

In The Price of Glory, Alistair Horne really brings to the page the ordinary human experience of Verdun. It’s just hell on earth. It’s this dystopian, mad landscape of destruction. And I think if John Keegan, in The Face of War, explains what battle feels like, this book explains how entire societies are pulled in to try and win what looks like a hopeless situation. Because that’s what happens. It’s what happens with the Soviet Union at Stalingrad in the Second World War. You manage to rouse the nation by declaring, ‘This is an existential threat. We could lose the country and be overrun if we are defeated.’

Verdun is, I think, the turning point for France. It saved the country in the Great War.

Let’s go on to the Pacific in World War II now, and you’ve chosen a memoir. This is With the Old Breed by E.B. Sledge.

This book is captured in the TV series The Pacific. It’s the Pacific version of Band of Brothers. A few years ago, I wrote a book called The Hiroshima Men, about the war in the Pacific and the race for the atomic bomb. To explain to my readers why you would drop an atom bomb on a city of human beings, I chart the progress of the war over three years and showcase how brutal it was – for the military as well as civilians. There was no quarter given, and no weapon off the table for either side.

The main character in the HBO series, Eugene Sledge, was a young U.S. Marine who doesn’t even enter the fighting until September 1944, but he’s then in some of the most vicious combat as American naval forces ‘island hop’ through the South and Central Pacific to establish bases close enough to bomb Japanese cities and ultimately invade the country. Equally, Japan knows that they must not allow this to happen or it will be unconditional surrender. That’s where the ferocity of their defence turns suicidal and casualties mount on both sides. American forces lost more men in the final year of the war than in the previous three years combined. That’s where Sledge’s memoir begins.

‘The Old Breed’ is a term given to veteran U.S. Marines, but these young, raw recruits like Sledge soon learn the art of war because of the brutality of the fighting on Okinawa and the fact the veterans already serving in their unit are being killed. It becomes about survival.

What I found emotive and why I chose it is that this book—above most other World War Two memoirs—is just incredible for capturing the psychological damage of being on the front line. It’s visceral. You can see why Tom Hanks’s production company based half the HBO series just on this single piece of biography, because the things Sledge witnesses, the fighting he experiences, his friends dying, the sheer waste of it all are perfectly captured in this memoir.

Sledge couldn’t write it when he came home. He was too damaged. It took him years to distil it, to then be ready to write down his epic tale. Most of the best World War Two memoirs, from an American perspective, started to come out in the mid-1950s because by then they could think, ‘I’m ready to put pen to paper.’ With the Old Breed is the standard against which you’d measure current memoirs. Are they as good as his? Because his is just extraordinary. And who knew? And I think it surprised him too. He’s such a gifted writer.

He went on to become a biology professor, I believe.

I’ve interviewed veterans from the Second World War on all sides in the process of writing my last two books, and there were quite a few who went on to have outstanding, stellar academic careers. There was one who was about to turn 100 when I spoke to him, he’s a professor at Colorado University. He was on Iwo Jima for three weeks and survived. He saw most of his friends killed and he said he jumped for joy when he realised they’d used the atomic bomb on Hiroshima. It took him years to understand just how terrible a decision that was. He said, ‘I regret it now but, at the time, I was 20 and I just wanted to live.’

A few months ago, I interviewed someone whose dad had been on the Burma Railway, and she’d just published his diary. She recommended the E.B. Sledge book as well, but I haven’t read it yet. I’m a bit scared to get to it.

You could watch the HBO series instead. It’s ten episodes and he’s in half of it. I honestly think the series really does capture the book because it’s so visual.

Let’s turn to your last book, A Soldier’s Song (1992) by Ken Lukowiak, which is about the Falklands War.

I was a young teenager when the Falklands War was on. I began my career in publishing in 1992, at a big London-based publisher. It was my first job and my degree was in history. I was surrounded by books and people would say ‘Just take one.’  You think, ‘Wow, it’s like Christmas!’ The publisher I was working for had just published this book.

A Soldier’s Song by Ken Lukowiak tells the story of what it was like to fight and survive down in the Falklands with the British forces. Lukowiak is an elite soldier, serving with 2nd Para. He’s been trained and highly conditioned to kill, and they did. They were very, very effective in the Falklands: arguably the best-performing unit.

It’s a bit like Sledge’s book, With the Old Breed, in that Lukowiak is adept at describing the fighting. But then it becomes almost like a novel from the 1960s where you’re finding the tragicomedy from Vietnam. Lukowiak’s candour and his humour are allied with emotional intelligence.

It paints a picture of what it’s like to switch from being bored for days on end because nothing’s happening, and then all of a sudden—bam!—you’re in the thick of the fighting. Bullets are flying around you in the dark and there is tracer fire everywhere. Your friends are dropping left and right. He captures that effectively, which is surprising because he’s not a trained writer, he’s a squaddie. Also, like Sledge, he wrote it years after the event. It’s about having the ability to put your mind back to that period you probably don’t want to revisit and bring it back to life.

At the time, I don’t think A Soldier’s Song was a bestseller. I have mentioned it a few times to people over the years, and they don’t know it. It’s still available secondhand on Amazon. It’s fantastic, and I’ve still got a copy that’s 30 years old at least. I see it as one of the most important books on the British side to come out of the Falklands campaign because, again, in a Keeganesque way, it’s talking about the ordinary soldier’s experience.

I haven’t read any books about the Falklands, and like you, I was pretty young at the time. What’s the story he’s telling?

The Falklands War began when Argentina’s military junta seized the islands in April 1982. Margaret Thatcher’s government rejected any suggestion of accepting the occupation and instead dispatched a naval task force to retake them. At the heart of the campaign were units such as the Royal Marines, the Parachute Regiment and the Guards, who faced the formidable task of advancing across difficult terrain towards Port Stanley.

Among them was Vincent Bramley Lukowiak of 2 Para, a battalion that found itself confronting well-armed Argentine forces entrenched on the high ground surrounding the capital. The British landed far from the main Argentine positions and had to march for days across bleak, windswept ground before assaulting a series of heavily defended objectives. The odds were often daunting, and while the British eventually prevailed, the victories came at a cost.

What makes Lukowiak’s memoir so powerful is that it strips away the patriotic headlines and triumphalism that followed the war. He takes the reader onto the battlefield itself: the freezing rain, the sodden peat bogs, the exhaustion, fear and uncertainty of combat. His story is not simply about military success, but about the human experience of war and the lasting physical and psychological burden carried by those who fought it.

Five Books aims to keep its book recommendations and interviews up to date. If you are the interviewee and would like to update your choice of books (or even just what you say about them) please email us at [email protected]

entries.title: Historical Novels About Women Written Out of History, recommended by Alice Jolly
entries.summary: Historical fiction can be both a valid and a valuable mode of examining unrecorded or forgotten figures in history, argues the award-winning novelist Alice Jolly. That is especially the case for women's history, which is so often thinly documented. Here she highlights five immersive novels that foreground female stories. This interview appeared first on Five Books.
entries.content:
Historical fiction can be both a valid and a valuable mode of examining unrecorded or forgotten figures in history, argues the award-winning novelist Alice Jolly. That is especially the case for women's history, which is so often thinly documented. Here she highlights five immersive novels that foreground female stories.

Thank you for selecting these five historical novels that bring to live the women who have been written out of history. In a previous interview, you described historical fiction as “an important subset within the mainstream of the writing and studying of history,” and I thought that was a striking way of framing it. Perhaps you’d expand on this point in the context of women’s history specifically.

Yes. It’s easy to reduce historical fiction to the period dramas we see on screens—where all the Elizabethan people have lipstick on. Whereas, actually, historical fiction really is important as part of the study of history. In particular, it can fill in the gaps in the mainstream historical accounts. It is often in the gaps that we find the women. Also, it can take us right into the minute so that we’re not looking at the past through hindsight.

We know women’s stories often don’t appear in the mainstream but we sometimes don’t see that women’s sensibilities have also been left out. An example of this appears in my novel, Mary Ann Sate, Imbecile. Mary Ann is a very simple woman, but she says: “Why are we always telling the story of what changes? Why don’t we tell the story of what remains the same?” And it’s true that mainstream history, almost by its nature, is about progress and conflict, and events that move things forward. Which is great, of course, but the people living through events often don’t experience them in that way at the time.

The novel I’ve just written begins with the words: “History isn’t history when it’s happening.” Whatever you live through, you just live through it, and it is only later that you may you realise that you have been part of it an extraordinary period in history.

I also feel very deeply about historical accuracy. So yes, we can centre women, but if we do, we mustn’t write bad history by giving women ideas and thoughts that they simply wouldn’t have had at the time. I don’t want history to be about picking out things from the past in order to make a point about the present. We need to really immerse ourselves in the thinking of the time.

You can’t just impose present-day narrative on to historical events. You can’t expect to walk straight through the door of a historical novel, you need to learn the language, accommodate yourself to what is going on because you are entering another world. The past is, literally, a foreign country, and the novel can ease us into modes of thought we might find uncomfortable, or ideas we no longer accept. That’s very exciting.

All of this sounds very relevant to your first book recommendation, which is Absolution by Alice McDermott. It’s set in a very specific community at a very specific time and place. And it foregrounds women that I’ve not seen much mention of in the history books. Would you tell us more?

Yes. These are women who are very peripheral, but they are located right where a momentous event is about to happen: the Vietnam War. The characters in this book are educated and progressive young American women who go with their husbands to Vietnam and live in a compound which is entirely American in style. Their lawns are green, as though they live in Westchester, and they live affluent lives. They have gardeners and cooks, and because they are liberal, they feel quite guilty about all this. But, of course, they enjoy it as well. They have fantastic social lives with cocktail parties and concerns about dresses, make-up and hair.

The writer is really coming at her subject matter through a side door because what lies behind all the superficial glitter is America’s disastrous attempt to ‘save’ the Vietnamese from communism. So, in this very closed world, we see the contradictions in the lives of these women. As one of them says, she was walking on air, but she “was not an airhead.” Aware of the poverty around them, they set out to do good.

There is an incredible memorable character called Charlene. She’s beautiful, clever, manipulative, but she’s also startlingly frank and practical. She wants to deliver little baskets of small luxuries to Vietnamese people to help them—because they are the lesser race, and it’s incumbent upon her, with her American college education, to offer them support. But as the novel continues, we realise there is something deeper going on. Charlene is also helping American women, back in America, who are unable to have children to adopt abandoned babies in Vietnam. The morality of this becomes horribly confusing and conflicted.

I loved this book, because it’s so slippery and tricky, so nuanced. It would have been easy to write a book where you hate these women, but you don’t—you sympathise with them, because they are trying to do something good, trying to support their husbands, trying to participate in the local culture, yet they can’t cross the cultural divide. And they can’t get away from a fundamental arrogance which makes them feel sure that America is a good society and that Americans know how to do thing the ‘right’ way.

The book is told by Tricia, who is looking back years at these events from many years later because she has been contacted by Charlene’s daughter who has questions about what was really going on in Vietnam. The question, I suppose, behind the book is: Is a white saviour better than no saviour at all?

Interesting.

Would it have been better for them just to leave people alone? Not to meddle? Yet they had a good motivation. The novel is really questioning the whole business of aid and also asking the reader to consider if there are some cultural boundaries we can never cross. It’s subtle and fascinating, while also being a gripping read. Also, it’s depiction of female friendships is deadly accurate and very uncomfortable.

I like a novel that allows us, as readers, to be on the ground as seismic historical events take place, or are about to take place. And I think that’s also true of your own multi-award-winning novel The Matchbox Girl, which is set in 1930s Vienna and features the real-life children’s hospital where Dr Hans Asperger worked. Could you talk a little about your research and where you saw potential for fiction?

It really began with Dr Asperger himself. This was around ten years ago. At that time there were very contrasting views of Asperger. Some of the darkest evidence against him had not yet come to light. I wanted to know who he really was. So that’s where I started but I soon found that some of the lesser characters were more interesting than Asperger himself. In particular, two women who were central to the first autism diagnosis had some how been forgotten, and I wanted to put them back at the centre of the story.

I didn’t have to skew history to make that happen, because it was all there in the documents. Women were very central to the work of the Curative Education Ward in Vienna, but that part of the story has been overlooked.

That’s interesting. It’s reminds me of a point made—if I remember correctly—by Elaine Showalter in the introduction to A Jury of Her Peers, in which she argues that major female authors have always existed, although their contributions have been omitted or erased for all sorts of reasons. There’s a mysterious, recurring amnesia about the role of women through history.

That’s right. In Vienna, they kept the records of doctors but not of nurses, and through that decision, the work of one very key person was lost. Another was Jewish and had to flee Vienna. Before she left, she had been carrying out work which really laid the foundations of the first autism diagnosis, and her contribution should undoubtedly be remembered.

Well, some women want their contributions to be lost to history; next we are going to discuss Angharad Hampshire’s The Mare, which was previously featured on Five Books when it was shortlisted for the Walter Scott Prize last year.

It’s a very interesting book. The woman at the centre of it, Hermine Braunsteiner, was a real person but she is a woman we would like to forget because she was a concentration camp guard, known for being extremely vicious.

The novel starts with a young American guy called Russell who goes on holiday to Austria and meets a seemingly pleasant young woman. This is Hermine. He marries her and they go back to the States. They are living a comfortable, normal life in suburban New York when a New York Times journalist knocks on the door and tells Russell who his wife really is. All of this is based on events that really happened.

What Angharad Hampshire has done is take us into the minds of these people. Part of the story is told through Hermine, part through Russell. It’s a story about denial. But what’s interesting is that we begin initially by feeling broadly sympathetic towards Hermine. We see her in Austria in the 1930s. She is a housemaid with no particular qualifications or abilities. Her whole life is going to be spent in low-grade domestic work. When she’s goes to Germany, she gets offered the opportunity to double her salary by working in a new prison for women that is just opening. She takes the job. Why would she not? But, as the story unfolds, we’re increasingly appalled.

As a character, Russell also becomes incredibly interesting. His sections of the book are addressed to Hermine, and they are like a love letter. He is devoted to her, and he will stay that way. No matter what is revealed about her, he still clings to her.

What makes this book so challenging is that you can’t quite dismiss these people. You want to say, well, she was evil and he was delusional. But you’re taken into their world. Hermine is extradited to Germany and stands trial. At the trial, she says: I’m being held scapegoat for a whole system. So many were involved, I took orders, I did what I was told, so why I am the one paying the price?

I’m somebody who has read many books about the 1930s and the Second World War. I’m always trying to answer the question of how people who are essentially harmless end up doing appalling things. This is the novel that has come closest to answering my question. It’s a clever, difficult, uncomfortable read.

And it raises questions about the power of fiction to create sympathy for unlikely people—real historical villains.

That’s right. The truth is, in terms of viewpoint, the person holding the microphone is the person in whom we make our emotional investment. That’s true even when we don’t like them. I think fiction becomes amazing when it forces us to empathise with a person we dislike. That’s an exercise that we need to go through, because simply saying, ‘these people are very bad people,’ doesn’t get you anywhere. The point is that Hermine was a woman like hundreds of other women. She was a woman like us, you know?

So it’s a thought-provoking book, and it’s also a propulsive read. These revelations unfold slowly. You keep thinking that, at some point, Hermine’s going to wake up to the real level of her guilt. You also except that at some point the author is going to tell us how terrible this all was. But the author is incredibly restrained. She lays it all out and leaves the reader to decide. Neither Hermine or Russell ever really confront the truth of what has happened, because they can’t, you know? At that point, suicide would probably be the only option.

Thank you. Your next book also explores morally complex characters, albeit in less extreme circumstances. Would you introduce us to Catherine Axelrad’s Célina? It features a chambermaid who enters into a sexual relationship with her employer, the author Victor Hugo.

Yes, this is a small press book and it is short, delicate, fragmentary. It was translated from the French by Philip Terry, who is an emeritus professor of creative writing at Essex University. He’s a wonderful translator.

Some years ago he translated this book because he really admired it, then he couldn’t find a home for it, so he had it sitting around for a while before he stumbled upon Les Fugitives, a wonderful small press that translates short French novels into English.

I think it took time for this book to find a home precisely because it is that work of historical fiction which makes no compromises in telling us what it really have been like to be a poor person living in that period. Victor Hugo himself remains peripheral. In fact, it isn’t even really mentioned that he is writing Les Misérables, although the reader figures that out.

This is also a book with a great sense of place. We feel the Channel Islands as isolated, cold, rocky, bleak. The sea is always heavy and grey, a damp mist always hangs low. The atmosphere is silent, serene, enclosed.

At the centre of this world is Célina, a maid servant whose life is tragic. Members of her family have died of tuberculosis, and she has been treated badly in her workplace. She gets the opportunity to take a job in the Hugo household, and this seems a good option for her but then she has an affair with Hugo. In reality, it isn’t really an affair: he simply turns up in her room every night to have sex with her.

This is a difficult book to read in the modern context. We want to feel outraged because this is a young and powerless girl having sex with a rather hideous older man who simply takes it for granted that having sex with the housemaid is his right. We feel outraged on her behalf, but she feels tenderly towards Hugo and enjoys the attention he briefly pays her. She is somebody who has so little in life that the idea of resisting him wouldn’t occur to her.

For her, it’s love, or at least she feels moved by him. Yet, equally, when she has the opportunity to have sex with somebody else who comes to the house, she does. So the novel is, among other things, a matter-of-fact account of a totally powerless woman who finds small pleasures where she can.

This novel maybe small and slight but it has huge impact and it is admirably restrained, wonderful quiet and beautifully written.

It’s a great recommendation, because it’s not a book that had been on my radar at all. Could we talk next about Ædnan? It’s described as an “epic, multigenerational novel-in-verse” about two Sámi families over the course of a century. Let me note for our international readers that the Sámi are the indigenous reindeer-herding people of the far north in Norway, Sweden, Finland and part of Russia.

This novel sounds as though it will be a big, challenging read, and it does cover a huge amount of ground but, actually, there are very few words on the page. The verse is fragmentary, leaving masses of white space. This creates a sense of the snow fields, visually, on the page.

It sounds like a dense read, and in a sense it is, because the language is poetical, lyrical. But the reader actually sails through it easily. Although it is epic, there is no sense in which it works through whole life stories. It’s more highly fragmentary focusing on tiny moments taking place amidst the vast landscape.

I absolutely loved this book. There’s a lot of references to Norse mythology. In Norse mythology there is always a leader or hero, but here the hero is the land itself, which is Ædnan. It’s about the people and their relationship with the land.

The Sámi have been caught up over many decades in the complicated politics of the far north. Also, at some point, in Sweden in particular, there were decisions aimed at ‘improving’ the Sámi. Their reindeer-based way of life came to seem problematic and the children were taken and put in residential ‘nomad’ schools— the contradiction there is obvious and, you know, that’s not going to go well, is it?

Their culture is lost or fragmented, because much of it was never written down. The youngest generation try to record their history, but it’s very hard to do. This book is, in part of an attempt, I suppose, to find a way to recreate history that really doesn’t exist any more.

I wouldn’t say the purpose of the novel is to centre women, but the women are very strong characters who try to hold the families and the culture together. The end of the book is quietly optimists, because the Sámi are actually taking the Swedish government to court to try to recover the land that they lost.

I just loved reading this book as it has a great atmosphere of the far north. I also appreciated the fact that it’s about how you can write down on paper something that can’t be written down. So it’s original and interesting and brave, as well as being a real pleasure to read. It’s both sad and uplifting, because it’s about the near-death of their culture and then the gradual revival, and the desire to tell their history. It’s a very unusual book.

Another great recommendation, thank you. And I think it might bring us to our last book, Deborah Moggach’s Tulip Fever, which brings us to 17th-century Amsterdam.

This book is set around 1630, the time of Vermeer, so we already have a visual idea of this society through the amazing paintings of the time, which are so serene and intimate and domestic. At the centre of this book is a young woman called Sophia who has been married off to a much older merchant called Cornelis. She’s quite glad about that because she comes from a poor family and she will live in comfort.

Cornelis commissions a marriage portrait from a painter called Jan, and when Jan comes to paint this portrait it’s not entirely surprising that he and Sophia begin to have a relationship.

This is all set against the backdrop of Tulip Fever, a period in the history of Amsterdam when people became utterly obsessed with tulips. It was like the South Sea bubble, or the modern dotcom bubble, even the AI bubble—a moment where everyone piles in to invest, with the promise of making a huge amount of money.

So the novel is about greed and lust, and how Sophia becomes entirely immoral in how she schemes to get out of her marriage and start a life with Jan. What really fascinated me about this book is the viewpoint. Usually, as a novelist, you either choose a very intimate viewpoint, a one-character viewpoint, which makes the book intimate and internal. Or, you choose a much wider viewpoint with many different characters and the opportunity to give a view of the whole city. What is extraordinary is that the writer switches between these approaches in a way which is deft and surprising and highly effective.

She said that the book was written quite quickly, which surprises me. It doesn’t read like that. My god, her instinct for how to put this thing together was absolutely accurate. You really get both: investment in all the characters, but also this overview of Amsterdam at that time.

It’s a dark story about illusion and deception, what you see and don’t see. It’s not a positive view of love, because the relationship between Sophia and Jan is utterly obsessive. She becomes prepared to do awful things to make it work. But it also has that serene Vermeer quality, with a sense of the intimate lives of people in their houses, the feel of the city and its canals. She packs so much into what is actually a relatively slim book. I really wanted to unpick the writing of it, the way she moves back and forwards across time, space, character.

When you are looking for an idea for a novel, do you start with the setting or characters or story?

I don’t really have a rule, but one thing I’m always looking for is moral ambivalence.

What I love in a novel is to finish reading and think: I’m not quite sure what to make of that. I’m not sure what I’m meant to think about these characters. That’s there in Absolution, with Charlene taking babies from an orphanage to give them lives with American women desperate to have children. These moral questions always attract me.

That comes through in the books we’ve discussed. What also comes through is the sense of people making calculations, figuring out what makes sense for them in the moment. I suppose that’s something universal to all of us, whatever period we live in.

That’s right. And so often we are not considering the bigger picture. Looking back, we might think: Were they not aware of this, or that? But there is so much we just aren’t thinking about, or don’t know about, even today with the internet. We make the decisions that are good for us in the moment, we get through the day, we survive.

Alice will be appearing in conversation with Heather Morris at the OzLit Festival at Foyles, Charing Cross on 18 October, 2026. Tickets are available here.

Pritchett Memorial Prize, and been longlisted for the Ondaatje and Rathbones Folio Prizes. She also currently teaches on the Creative Writing master’s programme at the University of Oxford.

entries.title: What is a memoir? Five examples of the genre, recommended by Jenny Evans
entries.summary: When Jenny Evans was writing her memoir, Don't Let It Break You, Honey, she read lots of other memoirs to figure out how best to go about it—studying how their authors shaped a life into a story, recreated the past and navigated the line between memory and fact. Here, she shares the five memoirs that taught her the most. This interview appeared first on Five Books.
entries.content:
What is a memoir, in your view?

It is a factual account of somebody’s life where the writer enters a contract with their reader, saying, ‘I am going to be true to the facts as I remember them, and the emotional truth will remain.’ But we must all accept that memory is fallible and that people can have differing interpretations of the same experience.

Memoir usually has something to say about not only the personal but also the political, or a wider point to make.

That’s what I liked about your book—not only was it a memoir about your life, but it was also an investigation into a really important story about the tabloid press in the UK, and how unscrupulously they can behave.

Yes, and that’s why it was commissioned. It’s a personal and inside take on a story which landed in the public consciousness as the ‘phone hacking scandal’ and something to do with Hugh Grant’s voicemail. It’s actually a police corruption scandal, at its heart. That was the real betrayal—the fact that there was illegality on a widespread scale happening at Murdoch tabloids and others, and the police helped cover that up.

That’s where my direct interest was because I had reported a crime to the police—and private details of that crime were then printed in the Sun newspaper. So I trained as a journalist to find out how that happened.

I had had other traumatic experiences too. I felt a bit sorry for the commissioning editor, Emma Smith at Little, Brown, when I was delivering it to her because I thought, ‘She’s expecting an investigation, and she’s going to get dead dad, dead brother, dead baby.’ But it’s a life, and what can you do? That is my experience. And despite that being my experience, I consider myself a very lucky person. I’m a loved person. I have never been neglected. I have always been caught when I have fallen. I have sought and found incredible friends. I have a very strong love from the family members who have survived. I’m a lucky person and I really hope that that comes across.

The examples of memoirs you’ve chosen are also nearly all about trauma, to some extent. Is that an important aspect of memoir?

Not necessarily, although I have chosen books by women, and I think that women are probably drawn both to read and write memoir to express our experiences of being a woman and of womanhood. And who lives a life without trauma? No one.

What I tried to do was reverse engineer these books and work out how the writers constructed them. I ended up massively intimidating myself and thinking, ‘I can’t do this! These are amazing!’ — but nevertheless, finding my own pathway and my own voice in the end. I kind of had to give up trying to be as good as everyone else and just write.

You come across as a very determined person—first you became a journalist; later you trained as a lawyer as well—all to get to the bottom of what happened.

It was much messier than that in reality. Part of my wanting to be a lawyer was because I’d been working on a story journalistically and I thought it might be a civil case, for example. I tried to encourage my sources to gather together and bring that case, but they wouldn’t do it without me. Or couldn’t, maybe. Trauma again. You need to feel safe to be able to act. That pushed me over the edge. I was like, ‘Fine. I’ll train to be a lawyer, and I’ll do it with you.’ There are many reasons why these things happen.

One of the weird things about writing out your life is that you begin to see yourself and the decisions you have made in patterns and themes. The reason I trained in law, it is clear now, and the journalistic story I mentioned falls into this, is that I have become very interested in ‘institutional abuse’ and means of accountability. Powerful institutions and organisations are well set up to protect themselves from criticism at this point. I had seen through my work with lawyers like Tamsin Allen of Bindman’s, on phone hacking, that the law, used creatively, has a good chance of puncturing those walls of self-protection. You can use legal frameworks to find discrepancies and sometimes compel answers in a way journalists are locked out from unless they have a whistleblower. That is very interesting to me.

With journalism, yes, I wanted to find out how this thing—details about a sexual assault I reported to the police ending up in the press—had happened to me, I definitely did. And I trained as a journalist to find out, but I was also motivated by the power asymmetry and wanting to redress the balance in some way. I had felt – experienced – the huge amount of power wielded by the people who had control of information, and I wanted some of that too. I wanted to regain some control, to grab some power. I wanted someone like me, who felt she had integrity, to be out there being a journalist, as well as those guys.

So there were many reasons for me to train both as a journalist and as a lawyer. But of course, when you’re writing a memoir, you boil it down to a nice, neat narrative. You tie it with a bow when, in fact, life isn’t like that.

What’s also interesting is that journalists are so often portrayed as a force for good, uncovering scandals. But in this case, they did some terrible things.

Yes, but I understood the pressures they were under. The system they were working in was incredibly misogynistic and full of male and white privilege. I understood why they had found themselves doing the things they had done. I found within the tabloids many highly intelligent, talented journalists with integrity.

I suspect the people who got higher up that chain lacked or perhaps lost integrity. With a nod and a wink, some of them encouraged criminality—in unlawful means of gathering information, such as phone hacking—and expected to get away with it because they were so well in with the police. Then, when their foot soldiers got caught, they did not take accountability, but instead threw the reporters under the bus.

It’s really the higher-ups—the executives and the desk heads—that I would say are responsible for what happened, or happens, within tabloid culture. Individual reporters were responsible for their actions too. But some were working in a culture where refusing could cost them their job. That matters when we ask who created and sustained that culture. Some left the industry; others tried to cling on because they wanted to be journalists and were good at their jobs. It’s not always easy to see clearly how toxic your working environment has become.

I lived overseas at the time and also thought the phone-hacking scandal was just something to do with Hugh Grant, but once, when I was passing through Heathrow, I picked up a book called Dial M for Murdoch by Tom Watson and Martin Hickman. It was so shocking. I kept telling everyone I met to read it. Like everyone, I was deeply affected by the story of Milly Dowler. I just couldn’t believe it.

It’s extraordinary. And Murdoch has kind of got away with it: he’s still one of the most powerful men in the world. As much as we could, we did a good job of exposing it, especially Nick Davies, but his tendrils reach far into establishments across the world.

Nick was actually one of the first people we interviewed on Five Books, back in 2009 or so, when we started. Several of us were journalists, and we thought, ‘Who would be the best person to interview on good books on being an investigative journalist?’ Still, despite all the public outrage, I don’t think the Leveson Inquiry’s recommendations were ever implemented.

Leveson Part Two—which was meant to be the investigation on the relationship between the police and the press—was cancelled. The Leveson Part I recommendations were accepted to a degree. From memory, David Cameron said something like it was going too far to regulate the press. I think that’s a fallacy, because TV journalism is regulated by Ofcom. It’s perfectly reasonable.

Let’s turn to the memoirs you’re recommending, examples of the genre on which you modelled your own. Let’s start with The Rules Do Not Apply by Ariel Levy.

The Rules Do Not Apply is about Levy’s life. The title is so clever. She was brought up unconventionally, and she has always tried to make the world work for her, rather than the other way around.

The key is that she lost her baby at 19 weeks. Her writing about that is just so incredibly beautiful. As someone who lost a baby at 27 weeks, I found it the most validating thing I’ve read in that space.

What she describes feels, at first, like a memoir of collapse. It’s not just about pregnancy loss; it’s about the marital breakdown of her parents, and her own; it’s a kind of shattering. But the book hints at the end that even though she lost her baby, she’s met someone new, and that she’s able to make a life even though the rules do not apply. Her life is unconventional, but she’s able to rebuild. I find that inspirational.

Do you think that’s the reason we read memoir – when we go through something, we feel like we’re the only one feeling it. And then when you read it in someone’s memoir, you realize you’re not alone?

Absolutely. All writers write because they’re seeking connection in some form. Even if they’re writing a murder mystery, they seek community. It’s an art form like any other. It’s about expressing yourself and seeing if you can find connection with others. We are looking for validation. At the same time, we might be looking to understand the counter point of view.

We all enjoy a narrative arc that ends in hope. My own book falls into it ever so slightly. We seek this hope that everything will be all right in the end. It’s not what real life is like. Life is messier than that.

Let’s go on to the next memoir you’ve chosen, Educated by Tara Westover. This was a huge bestseller, about growing up in a strict Mormon family.

Again, a very unconventional childhood, which she is encouraged to explore through academia in the end.

Educated is interesting because there are people who have questioned her version of events. A memoir is one person’s truthful account of events as they understood and experienced them.

I think memoir is really interesting because, beyond all other genres, it leaves you open to shame. Your credibility can be questioned, but what allows your credibility to be questioned is very gendered. We experience shame so viscerally as something wrong about us, but I often think that it belongs to the systems that got us into it in the first place. The same expectations we place on women elsewhere follow us into the way we read their memoirs. We judge whether they were good daughters, good mothers, whether they behaved as we think they should. Those judgments can become judgments about whether we believe them. It makes you very vulnerable to write a memoir —especially as a woman.

I found Educated intimidating because Westover is so clever. At times, though, I wondered how particular episodes served the larger story. It made me think about selection: how much do we include because it happened, and how much because it helps us tell the story?

In Ariel Levy’s writing, her scenes are vivid, but they’re never overwritten. She chooses one or two details rather than loading a scene with texture. It’s probably because she’s a journalist, but it is impactful. They’re just different ways of storytelling, I suppose.

I think Tara Westover is in this tough situation in that she’s writing about her family, and then it’s her family who challenges what she’s written.

We will come on to this with The Salt Path, but what do we expect? What is the contract we have entered into with writers of memoir? How much is truth, and how much is allowed to be poetic license or emotional truth?

Educated is set in Idaho, which she sounds beautiful in her descriptions. In your book, you write about growing up in Wales and your childhood.

Yes, it’s presented as slightly idyllic. My mum read the first draft and she said, ‘God, you’ve romanticized your childhood a bit, haven’t you?’ And I was like, ‘No, that’s how I see it, because I was the child. You were having a failing marriage and stressed about being a grown-up. I wasn’t.’

Tara Westover is similar to Maya Angelou, who is next on my list. The way they write is novelistic. The means by which they are able to convey what’s in their minds, the recall, is way beyond me.

Let’s move on to Maya Angelou now, because she is like a lodestar, a thread through your own memoir. Tell me about her 1969 autobiography, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings.

So I read that when I was young, and I reread it when I wrote my book, and listened to the audio version as well. Maya Angelou is a poet. She’s so careful with her language. She does write in detail, but it’s not necessarily the precision, it’s the authority of her voice and the emotional and moral truth of what she’s saying that gives it its power.

She communicates very directly and simply, almost in a populist way. She was an activist, and she’d have been a brilliant politician. She appeals to your emotions and that’s why she appeals to young people, I think, and is so endlessly quotable and instagrammable.

When I first read her book, I was grieving heavily for my dad. I was probably about 15 when I met her. I was struggling with how vulnerable bereavement and grief make you feel, and the strength with which you have to present yourself to the world, especially as a teenage girl. When I was in her presence, she was absolutely magnetic. A kind of stoic vulnerability. I was blown away by the fact that she wore her vulnerability as strength.

And when she left the stage she was speaking on – I had been to see her talk at the literature festival in Hay-on -Wye – she called me to her, wrapped me into a hug and whispered, ‘Don’t let it break you, honey. Don’t let it break you.’ Then she gave me her incredible smile. I have never forgotten it. Who would? So that became the title of my book. Maya-inspired.    

Going back to why we read memoir, I just saw who I aspired to be in her.

What’s so wonderful about memoirs is that you also learn about totally different lives – like hers, being brought up by her grandmother in the American South in the 1930s and 1940s. That also is what keeps me reading.

It’s so beautifully drawn and so novelistic from her. What I found when I was reading both her book and Tara Westover’s—because, as I say, I was trying to reverse engineer them—was, ‘How are they remembering the wind was blowing a certain way? There must be poetic license in this.’

But then I found, when I started writing my own, that I could close my eyes and picture myself there. Your brain does offer you these little details, like a pigeon pecking at the paving, or a fingernail worrying the flaky paint on a bench. I couldn’t tell you whether that is 100% the truth or not, but it very much felt like it was to me. It was like I was reliving the scene, and it was all coming back. I was also having EMDR therapy while I was writing. I found that revisiting these scenes brought back more detail than I had expected.

I suppose we think of things in headlines. I don’t know how we file things away in our brains, and maybe we all do it differently, but I think I had them as folders with titles on them. And then, when I went back and retrieved the folder to try, and put myself back in, say, the British Museum, with a particular source, I found there was loads of detail in there.

After that I thought, ‘Okay Angelou, Westover, maybe you did remember which way the wind was blowing that day. I think there’s a difference between honestly remembering something imperfectly and knowingly changing what happened. You can be truthful about your experience without claiming that your memory is infallible. But emotional truth isn’t a licence to invent the facts.

Before we get to that, let’s talk about A Life of My Own by Clare Tomalin. She’s a famous biographer of other people, but here she’s telling her own story.

I absolutely love her biography of Dickens, and for many years, it was my go to when I couldn’t sleep at night: ‘I’m going to listen to my Dickens audiobook.’

She does write about herself more like a biographer. Her writing is quieter and more restrained than some of the others, but it’s about grief and work and ambition and endurance. She doesn’t seem interested in romanticizing her life. It’s all quite clean and English and maybe cautious, but it’s an incredible life, really, and quite unsentimental. I don’t know if that is an English thing too, or a class thing.

I was drawn to it because I love her biographies. I wanted to see what she would do with her own life. And she basically did herself as she would have done someone else, I think.

Some terrible things happen to her, don’t they?

Her daughter dies by suicide and her husband, who was a foreign correspondent, has lots of affairs and then is killed. She had a profoundly disabled son, but she does lots of work to make their house work for him.

She has this incredible career in newspapers and it’s just an example of perseverance and determination, really—not that she ever makes a big deal out of that. She keeps going, without making a great declaration of her resilience. I admire that restraint.

Let’s turn to the final memoir you’ve recommended, The Salt Path, which was a huge success and turned into a movie before garnering some less positive attention. For those who haven’t come across it, can you say what it’s about?

It’s about a couple who—we are told—lose their family home because of a technicality in a court case. They have made the wrong investment after being duped by an old friend. In their 50s, with no home and no money, they decide to become vagabonds, essentially, and to walk the South West Coast Path with just their backpacks. At the same time, they discover that the husband has a very serious degenerative illness.

So it’s really a story of multiple journeys, both a physical journey along the South West Coast Path and also through his illness and facing up to that, and their loss of everything they built up in their lives and what that means.

It’s a beautifully written book, and when I first read it I was blown away by the prose. Subsequently, the Observer’s investigation raised serious questions about the account of how they lost their home. Winn has disputed the reporting. For me, that raises a really important question about the contract between a memoirist and their reader.

If you change the circumstances to make yourself appear blameless, that is a different thing from remembering a conversation imperfectly. I still think it’s a really interesting example of memoir, because it raises the question of how honestly we can write about things we feel ashamed of.

There have also been questions about the account of her husband’s illness, which they have disputed. I’m interested in what readers take from a story in which walking appears to bring recovery from serious illness. That is a powerful promise, and it matters how accurately it is presented.

So that space where memoir sits between reality and memory becomes a tug of war. The statement she has made via her lawyers is that it remains the ‘true story of their journey.’ Is that enough if the facts are incorrect? If the central circumstances have been misrepresented, I think that breaks the contract. I think people will accept that you can’t remember which way the wind is blowing, necessarily, or that memory is fallible and that not all of it will be verifiable facts. But you can’t knowingly change the facts to make yourself appear blameless. You have to own up to your fallibilities and bad decisions too.

But you’re still recommending it…Do you rate it as a book?

I thought her writing was beautiful, so on one level, I do. But the distinction matters. Fiction gives you the freedom to invent. With memoir, you are asking people to trust your account of what happened.

But if she’d written ‘I got into trouble because I stole some money,’ would that have worked as a story a publisher would be interested in?

There is a way of writing in which you own your terrible decisions. A story in which someone acknowledges wrongdoing can still offer a redemption arc. It becomes the journey within you to accept that you are fallible and can do bad things, that you owe apologies and can still forgive yourself and find beauty in the world. There is a version of that kind of story that I think would be very valuable.

But you have to be willing to look at the parts of yourself you would rather avoid.

In the end you the title of your memoir is Don’t Let it Break You, Honey, which gives a good indication of what you were up against. But you said you nearly called it Shame. Could you explain a bit more about that?

Shame can be one of the things trauma leaves you with. For me, it makes you want to hide. Guilt says, ‘I have done something bad.’ Shame says, ‘I am something bad,’ and sometimes, ‘That’s why these things happen to me.’ Talking about it with people who respond with care can begin to loosen its hold. For me, writing was part of that.

What I began to see when I was investigating this story—the ‘phone hacking scandal’— was the systems that create and perpetuate shame. Shame is a control mechanism, and it is used against women in very particular and powerful ways. The phone hacking scandal was a very misogynistic scandal, make no mistake. The tabloids are misogynistic. The way that they treated their female reporters was misogynistic and dangerous, as is the way that they portrayed and portray women. Also, the way they treated their sources, including women who reported crimes.

So women would report sexual violence as carried out by a famous person—as happened to me—and then the tabloids would offer them a huge amount of money to shed their anonymity and to talk about it in the pages of the newspaper. Then they would call them up on the day of publication and say, ‘Sorry, we’re not going to pay you because we don’t believe you. If you have a look at your contract, it says, if we don’t believe you, we don’t have to pay you.’ Then they would publish the story, and shame her.

As I say in my book, shame is the fuel on which the tabloids’ engines run. I began to see it as a construct sewn into this whole system. Rebekah Brooks is very senior in the Murdoch company, but mostly these were men. At the top of the police, it was almost all men. It seemed to me that they were all embroiled in this kind of shame-soaked battle. Tabloid reporters of old would take a load of coke, and then they would shame someone for selling coke. Or they would use sex workers, and then shame sex workers. They were making decisions, sometimes illegal decisions, sometimes unethical decisions, because they wanted to remain part of that group and retain their power.

And tabloid reporters behaving unethically or illegally to escape the shame of feeling they don’t belong, or have relinquished power in some way is one thing, but police – senior police – is quite another.

They have a duty to the rest of us to behave ethically, whether that’s to take care of us or whether that’s because they are part of a system that is designed to hold people to account. To break that contract to stay in a boys’ club with tabloid executives is – is it unforgivable? I think many police I know would say that it is. And these particular connections, at that particular time, were exposed, mostly by Nick’s hard work, so jobs were lost and apologies offered, but there’s a lot of work to do to dismantle those boys’ clubs today. It’s very dangerous.

How do you feel now, having written the book? Are you happy you did, or do you sometimes wish, ‘oh, gosh, I wish it wasn’t all out there’?

I feel many things at once. I was carrying a lot of shame about what has happened to me. I’ve experienced multiple instances of sexual violence over my lifetime, all of which leave you with a healthy dollop of shame. Also, the fact that I wasn’t considered worthy enough of respect for the police to keep my secrets, or that the tabloids would keep them, that I could just be used as so much fodder, left me with a lot of shame.

I thought most people’s response to the book would be, ‘Oh, wow, how interesting this investigative narrative is.’ Actually, most people who’ve written—and I get quite a lot of messages and DMs—say they saw themselves in the shame. People don’t write about shame because of the nature of it – it makes you want to hide. So I feel really there is a catharsis in writing about shame and shedding it. There is power in saying ‘I feel it too. And it doesn’t belong to me. I belongs to the person, or organisation, or institution that hurt me’. That is my version of Maya Angelou’s stoic vulnerability. I still feel exposed, and afraid of the book being used to shame me. Writing this stuff makes you vulnerable. Being a memoirist makes you vulnerable. But we should keep talking anyway, because there is power in community, and talking brings community.

You’ve been so incredibly brave about everything that’s happened—from reporting it and then sticking with it and fighting it. I mean, every step of the way, the instinct must have been to run away and not think about it, but you didn’t. You dealt with it.

But of course you don’t feel brave. You feel like shit, and you’re doing it because you feel like shit, and you just want to feel different and better. And you’re like, ‘Maybe if I get an answer, maybe if I find out the truth, maybe if I expose the bad person, I will feel less shit.’ It’s a survival mechanism in me, I think. Maybe I need to learn when I’ve done enough.

It’s a really good book. It’s also got really strong elements that would make a great film. Is it going to be made into a movie?

It’s been bought. These things quite often get stuck in development, don’t they? But Empire Street Productions, which has a strong feminist value system, has the rights. They work with Lily Allen, Self Esteem, Jodie Comer, Suzi Miller. I hope that means it’s got a good chance.
